column5: Dartmoor's allowance rests on statute: s10(1) Dartmoor Commons Act 1985 gives the public a right of access to the Commons on foot and on horseback for open-air recreation; the Supreme Court held unanimously (judgment 21/05/2025) that this includes wild camping, subject to the byelaws. Landowners cannot sue a camper in trespass while the byelaws are kept (paras 1-2, 17, 60).
The Commons are privately owned unenclosed moorland with commoners' grazing rights, about 37% of the National Park and 75% of its moorland (para 6). So the camper is a guest on working grazing land.

Byelaws (1989) para 6: no vehicle, caravan or structure other than a tent for camping on access land; Schedule 2 lists areas where camping is prohibited. Confirms 'no vehicle stays' and explains why the map must be checked (para 8). Byelaws also regulate fires and dogs (para 9).

Legal history: High Court 2023 ruled no right to camp; Court of Appeal 2023 reversed; Supreme Court 2025 dismissed the landowners' appeal (para 4, ch-002 para 60). A good applied case: guidance dated 2023 may be out of date.

Contrast: the Law of Property Act 1925 s193 gave public access to metropolitan commons for air and exercise but expressly excluded any right to camp or light a fire (para 36). An access right does not automatically include camping; check the instrument.

Byelaws can be changed and the Park Authority can close parts of the Commons by notice for protection or restoration (s10(4), para 29), consistent with the course's 'check the local rule before you go'.
